title: Baseline correction using asymmetrically reweighted penalized least squares smoothing

citations.claim: Baek et al. proposed the arPLS (asymmetrically reweighted penalized least squares) method, which uses a generalized logistic function to assign weights that give similar importance to signals slightly above and below the estimated baseline, thereby avoiding the baseline underestimation problem of earlier methods.

Baek et al. showed that AsLS and airPLS methods systematically underestimate the baseline in non-peak regions because they assign zero or near-zero weight to all signals above the fitted baseline, causing downward bias and peak height overestimation.

The arPLS weighting scheme uses the mean and standard deviation of negative residuals (signals below the current baseline estimate) to parameterize a generalized logistic function that smoothly transitions weights from one (baseline region) to zero (peak region).
Baek et al. demonstrated that arPLS achieved approximately half the RMSE of AsLS and airPLS on simulated spectra with known ground-truth baselines, for both low-noise and high-noise conditions.
Baek et al. showed that arPLS is relatively robust to the choice of the smoothness parameter lambda, maintaining low RMSE over a range spanning more than two orders of magnitude.
The arPLS method, like AsLS and airPLS, still requires manual selection of the smoothness parameter lambda, which must be tuned per application.
Baek et al. formulated baseline correction as the weighted penalized least squares problem z = (W + lambda*D'D)^{-1} Wy, iteratively updating the weight matrix W until convergence.

do_not_claim: Baek et al. proposed the penalized least squares framework for baseline correction (this was proposed by Eilers and Boelens in 2005)
arPLS eliminates all user-specified parameters (it still requires the smoothness parameter lambda)
arPLS was designed for chromatographic baseline correction specifically (it was developed for and tested on Raman spectra)
